5eaf464e45df768f: The world’s most important shipping lanes pass through the Strait of Malacca.
Yet, within Malaysia’s maritime boundaries, there is no single framework to determine who gets to use which patch of water and for what purpose.

That shortcoming was the subject of discussion at a recent Ensearch forum “Our Seas, Our Future” where Dr Gopinath Nagaraj and Dr Harinder Rai Singh of FanLi Marine and Consultancy Sdn Bhd (FanLi) made the case for marine spatial planning with a clarity Malaysia would do well to heed.
Their framing of the sea as overlapping estates of biodiversity, fisheries, industry and maritime activity is right. The ocean is not just a shipping lane with some fish in it.
Their point is that fragmented governance, rather than a lack of awareness, is the real barrier.

The numbers bear this out: fisheries production was valued at RM11.43 billion in 2023, Malaysian ports handled more than 30 million TEUs in 2024, and offshore oil, gas and tourism all draw on the same finite waters.
Yet each sector is planned or managed by a different authority under a different law.
Fragmentation is not a natural disaster. It is a choice — the accumulated result of agencies guarding their own turf and a Cabinet unwilling to make one give ground.
The department of environment approves reclamation and coastal EIA reports one environmental impact assessment at a time. That is not enough.

Every silted estuary and buried mudflat in this country may have been approved through a valid EIA. Until the DOE requires cumulative-impact assessments — measuring the combined effect of projects along an entire coastline rather than assessing each project in isolation — its approval process risks certifying decline one project at a time.

The fisheries numbers tell another story. In 2022, marine landings totalled 1.308 million metric tonnes (mt), valued at RM11.3 billion. In 2023, they fell to 1.27 million mt, valued at RM11.43 billion. In 2024, they rose to 1.392 million mt, valued at RM11.84 billion, and in 2025 to 1.393 million mt, valued at RM11.88 billion.

The fisheries department holds the nursery-ground data any marine plan would need. Yet there is still no publicly available national fish-habitat atlas. Food security is its responsibility. Where is the map?
The marine department and the transport ministry plan sea lanes and port expansions as though reefs and fishing grounds simply are not there.
Navigation matters enormously, but it is not the only estate at sea. Too often, the ministry behaves like the senior claimant whose needs are settled before anyone else is consulted.
The malaysian maritime enforcement agency and the navy have the mandate to secure our waters. Yet illegal sand dredging, unpermitted reclamation and foreign incursions continue.
This is the half of the conversation too often forgotten: a marine plan without enforcement is a coloured map. Zoning that no one polices protects nothing.
State governments control the foreshore out to three nautical miles and monetise it through reclamation deals that federal ecological policy struggle to stop.

Every attempt at a “national” ocean policy eventually runs into this constitutional divide. Sabah, Sarawak and reclamation-hungry peninsular states cannot keep hiding behind the Federal Constitution while treating the coastline as an asset to be sold to the highest bidder.
PlanMalaysia (formerly known as the department of town and country planning) and local authorities have been told to extend spatial planning into marine areas.
Yet they lack both the statutory machinery and the planning expertise to do so effectively. Beyond the high-water line, they have done little.
Petronas operates across the same seabed designated for conservation, under terms negotiated federally, without having to reconcile its footprint within an integrated marine plan.
Its data can also become difficult to scrutinise when national security is invoked.
And above all sits the Cabinet. The draft National Ocean Policy, with its proposal for an oceans and fisheries ministry, has remained a draft for years.

This is not a technical shortfall. It is a decision no one has been willing to make because unification means one ministry losing authority to another. That is a failure of political will dressed up as a coordination problem.
The experts who advocated for marine spatial planning (MSP) can only diagnose and recommend.

Their prescription is sound: a national MSP governance unit with a real legal mandate; a marine data system and conflict atlas; pilot planning zones in Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak; and zoning developed through genuine consultation with fisherfolk who actually know the waters. It is the right blueprint.

But blueprints have never been the problem. Malaysia does not lack marine policy; it has too much of it, scattered across a dozen agencies, with none willing to surrender an inch and no single body empowered to force them to work together.
So the test is simple, and it is a test of government, not consultants.
Give one body three things: a legal mandate strong enough to override sectoral silos, a budget line in the next Malaysia Plan, and enforcement teeth on the water.
Most importantly, give it a political structure capable of bringing competing interests together.
The draft National Ocean Policy advocated such an approach. Drawing on a similar challenge faced by Canada, it proposed a ministry of oceans and fisheries.
Anything less, and the next forum will be another well-attended description of a problem we have all agreed on for a decade — held while the reclamation barges keep working just offshore.
The sea is a shared and finite national asset, not empty space reserved for the most powerful claimant. Right now, it has no ministry, no map and no enforcer of its own.
That is not the ocean’s failing. It is ours.

ce70dbb38957bdd7: I saw a social media post about a man so old he’s bent double but still doing motorcycle food delivery. Most comments on the post were positive and laudatory, seeing this as evidence that, in spite of advanced age, some people still want to be useful and be seen as “normal”.
Yeah, as normal as old people in developed countries working as cashiers at convenience stores or cleaning tables at fast-food joints.
I don’t buy that. If somebody of that age and physical condition is still running around delivering food, they aren’t doing it for fun or for the flex.

I'm a retiree. I’m not rich but I think I have “enough”, whatever enough is. It could turn out I don’t actually have enough and will end my days burdening others or, just as bad in my view, that I have more than enough -- which means I’ve wasted too much of my life acquiring wealth and not actually living it.

May I be spared these two calamities. I’m more inclined to believe that not having enough is the real reason the old bent-double man still runs around doing food deliveries. He’s not doing it for the fresh air or to meet new people.

And may you be spared that fate, too. Life gets tougher every day and not a single day passes that I don’t think about my good fortune of having retired and being able to approach 70 in relatively good physical and economic health. I also can’t help but think of those worse off than me every single day.

In the old days people didn’t really retire. They just stopped working when their body couldn’t handle it any more or when their grown-up children started taking care of them. Those who had actual pensions, mostly retired government employees, were the extra lucky ones.

I chose to retire in my early 60s with a year of my employment contract still to run. Things were changing at my employer's - the usual corporate transformation stuff - and it was best I left and let the new bosses choose my replacement themselves.

In effect I had a year-long pre-retirement leave: I have nothing to complain about and plenty to be grateful for. But some of my corporate peers chose to continue working, and I doubt it’s because they need the money. I surmise they need the job as a validation of some sorts – that 'Hey, I'm still needed and relevant and important'!

I don’t miss the good old corporate warrior days. What I do miss is the interaction with people at work, which I replace by making new friends while still keeping the old ones. Many still remember me and I never say no to a chance for a free meal and listen to them whinge about their bosses!

Through my career, I never took myself seriously. I earned enough to live a comfortable life and feed and clothe and educate my kids. My four decades of being a pen-pusher also gave me “enough” for my retirement, which I think is what running the rat race should be about.

Malaysia is still a country of young people but as lifespans increase there are an increasing number of people like me, comfortably retired and with years still ahead of us. But there are also many others like that old man who, allegedly, still does motorcycle delivery in spite of his advanced age and medical condition.

Having “enough” helps you be independent. There is life outside of work and that spared me the pain of leaving my title, office, and other perks behind. After all I wasn’t teaching the young or curing the sick or growing food or keeping society safe through unglamorous jobs as firemen or rubbish collectors. What I did for a living wasn’t really fundamental to the survival of our species.

Many middle-aged people, especially government servants, pray for an optional early retirement that can't come early enough. They’re probably stuck in a toxic work environment just to put food on the table and perhaps squirrel away some money for retirement. That’s not living - that’s just surviving.

That we’re a country of many young people still toiling away to create wealth for themselves, and hence for the country, is a blessing. Their labour ensures that our pension funds and investments and social safety nets such as public healthcare will still last at least for a few more decades.

However, the younger generation are not guaranteed a safety net and soft landing when they retire. We post-WW2 “Baby Boomers” are the wealthiest generation ever, but we may need that wealth to take care of ourselves and not burden our own children, whose own wealth and filial piety may not be enough to care for us.

Our generation’s wealth also unfortunately comes from destructive greed. We live a better life than our parents but the price of our good life comes from ruining the climate and depleting and defiling the earth’s resources and creating economic and social disparities. Such is the world we’re handing to our kids.

Apart from relationships and independence, health matters more as we age. We once traded our time and even health to make money. Now, we’re trying to trade money for time and health. But time and health are elusive and without some humility in our life perspectives, they still can’t guarantee a peaceful autumn of our life.

Ironically a solution for a happier final chapter perhaps lies in giving back to others. When I recall the old Japanese rescue workers at the Fukushima nuclear plant disaster as well as the elderly British protesters against the Gaza genocide who volunteered to be arrested in the UK, I choke up.

These brave old people purposely chose harm and danger for themselves to protect those younger than themselves. They had a good innings in the game of life, and are now willing to sacrifice to help the younger ones play their own innings. It’s the ultimate measure of having lived a good life that you’re prepared to lose it to protect others.

I’m extremely lucky I never had to make such a decision, or even have to be on a motorcycle to deliver food. I’d like to think I’d have discharged myself honourably if tested. But I’m in no hurry to put myself to these tests!
